title: A teacher and a friend (Avot 1:6)
hookLine: get yourself a teacher, gain a companion, and judge everyone favorably
carry: judge on the side of merit

lines: I NEED TO TALK. THEN SILENCE.
THE STORY IN HALF A SECOND.
cards: A friend texts, I need to talk, and then goes silent for six hours. A coworker walks past without saying hi. Your brother forgets your birthday.
Each time, your brain writes a story in about half a second. They're angry at me. They're rude.
He doesn't care. Sometimes the story is right. Often, it isn't.
The phone died. She was crying in the stairwell. He's drowning at work.

teach.b: Joshua ben Perachyah says, in paraphrase: make for yourself a teacher, acquire for yourself a friend, and judge every person favorably. Look at the verbs.
Make a teacher, not find one: even if no perfect teacher appears, choose someone and make them your teacher.
Acquire a friend: the Hebrew kneh means buy. A real friend costs you something: time, patience, the humility to be corrected.

An early companion to Avot says a true friend is someone you eat with, study with, and trust with your secrets. Jewish learning built this into its method. Students study in pairs, a chavruta, arguing over every line.
Now the third: judge every person favorably.

teach.h: LECHAF ZECHUT — ON THE SIDE OF MERIT.
teach.b: In Hebrew, lechaf zechut, on the side of merit. Picture a scale. When you don't know why someone did something, tip it toward the good reading.
The Talmud tells a story about it. A man works three years for a farmer. On the eve of the holiday he asks for his wages.
No money, the farmer says. Then give me produce. I don't have any.

The worker goes home empty-handed. After the holiday the farmer arrives with his wages and gifts, and asks: what did you think when I said I had nothing? Each time, the worker had imagined an innocent reason.
And he was right: the farmer had pledged all his property to the Temple, and had it undone.

teach.h: JUDGE ON THE SIDE OF MERIT.
teach.b: The farmer says: as you judged me favorably, may God judge you favorably.

how: Traditional Jewish study is often done in a chavruta, a pair of study partners who read and argue together, and dan lechaf zechut, judging others favorably, is counted among the everyday duties between people.

o: giving people the benefit of the doubt
ruling strictly by the letter of the law
earning merit by doing extra good deeds

games.q: three pieces of advice — tap the pairs.
p: acquire a friend, even at a cost

s: the Hebrew for acquire a friend can mean buy
kneh means buy or acquire: a real friend costs you something.
in the Talmud's story, the farmer really had no money
he'd pledged all his property to the Temple and had it released; he came back with wages and gifts.
Avot says to wait for the perfect teacher to find you
it says make yourself a teacher: choose one.

games.q: you've worked three years for a farmer. on the eve of the holiday he says he has nothing to pay you: no money, no produce, no land. what do you think?
o: there must be a reason I don't know.
games.why: in the Talmud's story, the worker imagined an innocent reason each time, and was right. the farmer said: as you judged me favorably, may God judge you favorably.

practice: Think of someone whose behavior bothered you recently, and, like the worker, come up with an innocent explanation, then a second, then a third. You don't have to believe them; just notice there's more than one story.
Let the scale tip, a little, toward merit.

wordCard.voice: Lechaf zechut. On the side of merit: Joshua ben Perachyah's call to judge every person favorably, tipping the scale toward the good reading.

orig.note: Hebrew: to the side of merit, the good side of the scale (Avot 1:6).

carryVoice: Your line: judge on the side of merit. A teacher, a friend, and a generous scale. That's day two hundred thirty-nine.
